prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and its development into an optical frequency standard at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B045 with Katori and Ye, as a single-part prize. After the first round I have tightened the reasoning rather than the conclusion. Johansson and Lindroth both argued that the citation must name the discovery as the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, not the 10^-18 number, and I now agree that this is the right way to separate the lattice clock from earlier prizes. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb that counts optical cycles and the laser stabilisation behind it; the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems and single-ion clocks. The lattice clock solves a different problem, the quantum-projection-noise limit, by interrogating thousands of atoms at once while the trap shifts, Doppler and recoil effects are cancelled. That is a method that opens a new regime of measurement, and its confirmation is built in because independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST are compared routinely and agree at the 10^-18 level. As an experimentalist I weigh that reproducibility, with centimetre-scale redshift measurements and constraints on constants and dark matter already obtained, above projected consequences. It is also the only shortlisted candidate where every member who discussed the credit reached the same names, so no choice among deserving people has to be forced.
statement.case_against: The reservations I raised in round 1 remain real. Distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is an argument the committee must decide, not dismiss; Danielsson, Mehlig and Eriksson are right that the headline is a measurement capability and that what the clock has taught us about nature is still partly prospective, with the redefinition of the second not yet done. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto in Katori's group, and Hall-type laser stabilisation, and I cannot verify the exact priority of the magic-wavelength proposal against the first strontium demonstrations from the supplied text. I also grant Mehlig's point that B040 changes how a whole field classifies phases, which a clock does not. Where I part from that view is that conceptual breadth is not the only criterion for a physics prize, and B040 still has an unresolved credit problem.

responses.point: Danielsson regards the lattice clock as an enabling precision tool whose learning about nature is prospective, and wants the redefinition of the second or a fundamental result to carry more weight, while preferring B016 because the neutrino flux told us something new.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between telling us something new and giving a better number, but I think the lattice clock already has results of the first kind: the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across an atomic sample, the many-body spin and interaction physics in the lattice, and tightened bounds on drifts of constants and ultralight dark matter. I would therefore not hang the citation on the redefinition of the second, which depends on metrological and political steps and would make the prize hostage to timing. On B016 I take your own point that it is mature only if the diffuse flux alone is the discovery. I would be content with that framing, but the Halzen and Karle split is not settled and neither you nor the Chair claims to settle it, so I keep B016 as my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that a topological classification changes how a whole field thinks and so outranks the clock on scientific grounds, and would not oppose B045 if a two-part prize were considered.
responses.response: I agree B040 is a conceptual advance of larger breadth, and I do not argue otherwise. My disagreement is about what we can award from the record. You name the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, Hasan's 3D spectroscopy and Zhang's death as unresolved and Eriksson and Olsson say the same, so the three-name limit forces an exclusion that the committee has not defended. Conceptual weight counts, but a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio would be challenged immediately by the 3D community, and the 2016 prize invites a continuation argument. I do not support a two-part prize as a way to avoid that choice: the three-name cap would shrink B040 further, and I see no scientific link between the parts. If the committee settles the B040 credit convincingly, I would move it above B016 among my alternatives, which is why it is now my second alternative.

responses.point: Johansson moved B045 to the top after reading the openings, but says B026 has the stronger claim to open a new regime and that his preference is partly a judgement on timing and robustness.
responses.response: I appreciate that you stated the timing element openly. I agree the citation should name the magic-wavelength trapping and not the accuracy figure, and I have changed my citation accordingly. On B026, I weigh the 2025 prize and your declared conflict as the reasons to drop it as my first alternative: with your recusal the committee would be deciding it with one fewer informed voice, and Girvin and Huang are not cleanly handled by the Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf trio. I also should say plainly that my own quantum-information and WACQT ties are an additional reason for me not to lead on B026 or B007. So I now list B016 and B040 as alternatives, where the credit problems are at least not conflicted by committee members.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, prefers B016 but accepts the diffuse-flux-only citation, concedes that the Halzen-Karle split cannot be settled from the text, and calls B045 the probable consensus candidate.
responses.response: Your own account of the attribution weakness for B016 is the main reason I keep it as an alternative rather than a preference, and I appreciate that you say you would cite only the diffuse flux. The point I would ask you to test is that a detector prize needs a record that the committee can check: who led the discovery analyses and whether the AMANDA-era leaders have a stronger claim. If the committee can answer that in favour of Halzen and Karle, B016 becomes a real contender for me and a fine second choice. On consensus, I would not treat B045 as the winner because it is widely second, but I do think the fact that its supporters, including those who prefer other ballots, agree on the two names is evidence about the strength of the credit, not just popularity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes once the citation names magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms.

Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly capture the decisive contributions given Lemonde, the SYRTE group, Takamoto and Hall-type laser stabilisation, and the exact priority of the magic-wavelength proposal.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, which would add practical weight but is not needed for the physics.
Whether the B016 or B040 credit problems can be resolved within three names, since either would then rival B045 as a first choice.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged and mild. I spent a year during my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's laser-stabilisation and comb work underlies the clock field and is linked to Jun Ye's group at JILA; I have no collaboration with, or supervisory relation to, Katori or Ye. My rare-earth quantum-memory work and my WACQT role overlap with the quantum-information ballots (B007, B026, B028) and with Chalmers, where Göran Johansson works, which is why I no longer put B026 or B007 among my alternatives. I do not consider any of this a recusal-level conflict for B045, B016 or B040.
